interactions.summary: Jiang answers the prior question by saying Greek spirits take possession of animals or people rather than arriving as stable material bodies, and he uses that pattern to explain Dante's Apollo invocation as a request for possession and poetic power.
A participant reads the Paradise passage in which Dante says passing beyond the human cannot be fully worded and Beatrice tells him he is already moving beyond earth and false imagining.

Jiang glosses the passage by framing Paradise as Dante's attempt to narrate a twenty-year-old visionary experience with Beatrice and by arguing that Beatrice's role is to strip away earthbound logic, ego, doubt, and fear so Dante can rely on intuition and imagination before meeting God.
A student asks whether the anti-logic move is an allegory for Christian apologetics about faith, and Jiang answers that Dante will address it later through Paul and a faith-without-evidence frame.
Another participant asks why logic would be unnecessary in heaven if communication still seems to require some shared rational structure.

claims.claim: Jiang says Greek spirits take possession of animals or people rather than appearing as ordinary material forms, and only through such possession can they perceive time and space.
Jiang interprets Dante's Apollo invocation as a request to be possessed so he can use Apollo's powers to describe what he saw.
Jiang says Dante is narrating, as a pilgrim, an extraordinary experience with Beatrice that happened twenty years earlier and exceeded ordinary imagination.
Jiang says the heavenly universe is presented in linearized form only so Dante can process it, even though it is fundamentally beyond ordinary time and space.
Jiang says Beatrice is telling Dante to rely on intuition and imagination rather than earthly logic when entering heaven.
Jiang frames the journey toward God as a process of dispelling false imaginings by letting go of ego, doubt, and fear.
Jiang says Paul later formulates faith as belief without evidence and signals that Dante will return to this issue later in the poem.

signature_moments.moment: Apollo is not just a literary allusion but a spirit Jiang thinks Dante wants to possess him.
signature_moments.source_phrase: he's trying to have Apollo possess him
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns poetic inspiration into a concrete metaphysical transaction rather than a decorative classical flourish.

signature_moments.moment: The way to God begins by dropping logic imported from earth and trusting intuition enough to let false imaginings fall away.
signature_moments.source_phrase: do not try to use logic
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is Jiang's sharpest formulation so far of why Paradise demands a different mental posture from ordinary reasoning.

signature_moments.moment: Beatrice's guidance is recast as an attack on ego, doubt, and fear before any meeting with God can happen.
signature_moments.source_phrase: let go of your ego. let go of your doubts. let go of your fear
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It makes the ascent spiritual and psychological at once, not just cosmological.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: A divine power Dante invokes, which Jiang interprets as a spirit whose possession would enable poetic speech.
Beatrice's name for the earthbound misconceptions Dante must shed before he can understand heaven properly.
Raised in class as the Christian mode tied to belief without evidence and deferred by Jiang to Dante's later treatment of Paul.

chronology_notes.note: Jiang explicitly marks the narrated ascent as a remembered experience from twenty years earlier within Dante's storyworld, so this packet contains internal chronology rather than an update to another dated Jiang source.
